title: ASIC warns scammers are using AI to spin vast webs of deception

reading.body:
An AI system was used to create a fake news article impersonating real public figures, the Reserve Bank governor and an ABC presenter, in order to promote a fraudulent investment scheme. The article described an interview that never occurred, using AI-generated or fabricated content to add false credibility to an unlicensed cryptocurrency platform. This represents deployment of AI technology for impersonation and fraud rather than its intended use.

The failure occurred at the point where AI-generated text entered the financial fraud ecosystem without any apparent human verification of its claims or authenticity. Catching this would have required either the AI system itself to refuse to generate fabricated interviews attributed to real people, or human review to confirm that the interview actually took place before publication. It is not established whether the fake article was generated by a single model prompt or assembled from multiple AI outputs.

The incident exemplifies a broader pattern: ASIC reported a 182 percent increase in scams involving AI-generated deepfakes and fabricated content in the prior year, with fake investment platforms rising 151 percent. The same impersonation approach has been applied repeatedly to a small set of prominent Australians, suggesting the technique is effective and reproducible at scale.

reports.title: The fake Alan Kohler interview that shows a type of scam that’s on the rise
AI deepfake scams 'an emergency in the making' as ASIC reports rise in false investment endorsements
ASIC warns scammers are using AI to spin vast webs of deception

summary:
# Summary

A fake online article featuring Reserve Bank governor Michele Bullock and ABC finance presenter Alan Kohler discussing a fraudulent cryptocurrency platform called Boulder Sparhaven exemplifies a rising scam trend. The article, which described an increasingly heated interview that never actually occurred, promoted an unlicensed investment scheme. ASIC reports that AI-generated deepfakes and fabricated content are becoming more prevalent and sophisticated, with the regulator removing 19,400 scams last year, a 182 percent increase from the previous year. Phishing scams jumped 279 percent, while fake investment platforms rose 151 percent.

The most commonly impersonated Australians include Prime Minister Anthony Albanese, broadcaster Alan Kohler, businessman Dick Smith, and mining magnate Gina Rinehart. Scammers create elaborate webs of deception using fake websites, news articles, positive reviews, and advertisements to lure victims. ASIC advises consumers to verify Australian Financial Services license numbers through official registers before investing. Alan Kohler suggests stronger penalties for platforms hosting this content and the AI models enabling it, noting that consumer warnings alone are insufficient.
